fact_checks.rationale: FDA/Drugs@FDA, FDA labeling, LiverTox, and PubMed records identify the drug as tiagabine/tiagabine hydrochloride.
FDA labeling and Drugs@FDA use the salt name tiagabine hydrochloride/tiagabine HCl. This should be captured as an alias so the salt name is not treated as a separate drug row.
Drugs@FDA lists Gabitril (tiagabine HCl), and LiverTox lists Gabitril as a representative trade name.
NO-328 is a documented tiagabine research/development alias.
FDA has an approved NDA for Gabitril/tiagabine HCl and FDA labeling is available.
Drugs@FDA lists Gabitril approval date as 9/30/1997.
FDA labeling indicates adjunctive therapy for partial seizures; ILAE/NCBI terminology supports focal as the current term corresponding to partial seizures.
FDA labeling lists 2 mg, 4 mg, 12 mg, and 16 mg oral tablets.

fact_checks.current_value: CNS: dizziness 27%, CNS: asthenia 23%, CNS: somnolence 21%, GI: nausea 11%, neurologic: tremor 9%, psychiatric: nervousness 8%
fact_checks.proposed_value: CNS: dizziness 27%, CNS: asthenia 20%, CNS: somnolence 18%, GI: nausea 11%, neurologic: tremor 9%, psychiatric: nervousness 10%
fact_checks.rationale: The FDA label pooled placebo-controlled add-on trial adverse-event table supports dizziness 27%, nausea 11%, tremor 9%, but lists asthenia 20%, somnolence 18%, and nervousness 10%, not 23%, 21%, and 8%.

fact_checks.current_value: Precise antiseizure mechanism is unknown, but tiagabine blocks GABA uptake by the GAT-1 GABA transporter, increasing synaptic GABA availability.
fact_checks.proposed_value: Precise antiseizure mechanism is unknown; tiagabine enhances GABA activity by binding to GABA uptake-carrier recognition sites and blocking GABA uptake into presynaptic neurons, increasing GABA available for postsynaptic receptor binding.
fact_checks.rationale: FDA labeling supports GABA uptake-carrier blockade and increased GABA availability, but the cited FDA label wording does not specifically name GAT-1.
GABA uptake inhibition is well established in FDA labeling and NCBI/PubMed pharmacology sources, despite the label noting that the precise antiseizure mechanism is unknown.
FDA labeling supports the mechanism. DailyMed should not be needed as the named source when an FDA label URL is available.

fact_checks.current_value: Not a major inducer/inhibitor; CYP3A substrate
fact_checks.proposed_value: Not a major inducer/inhibitor; CYP3A substrate
fact_checks.rationale: NCBI Bookshelf lists tiagabine as neither a hepatic enzyme inducer nor inhibitor, and a substrate affected by enzyme-inducing ASMs/CYP3A-mediated metabolism.
LiverTox and NCBI pharmacokinetic sources state that tiagabine is metabolized by the liver/hepatic CYP system.
PubMed review supports 5-8 h mean half-life and NCBI Bookshelf supports shortening to 2-3 h with hepatic enzyme-inducing ASMs.
FDA labeling states adult total daily dose may be increased up to 56 mg/day and that doses above 56 mg/day have not been systematically evaluated in adequate and well-controlled trials.

fact_checks.current_value: 16 mg/day common lower maintenance; titrate to 32-56 mg/day depending on enzyme-inducing ASMs
fact_checks.proposed_value: Start 4 mg once daily; titrate by 4-8 mg/week. Usual adult maintenance in enzyme-induced patients: 32-56 mg/day in 2-4 divided doses; lower/slower dosing is required in non-induced patients.
fact_checks.rationale: FDA labeling supports initiation at 4 mg once daily and usual adult maintenance of 32-56 mg/day in induced patients; it does not support 16 mg/day as a common lower maintenance dose.

fact_checks.current_value: Adjunctive focal seizures: 32-56 mg/day divided depending on enzyme-inducing ASMs
fact_checks.proposed_value: Adjunctive focal/partial seizures: 32-56 mg/day in 2-4 divided doses in enzyme-induced adult patients; lower/slower dosing in non-induced patients.
fact_checks.rationale: FDA labeling supports 32-56 mg/day in two to four divided doses for induced adult patients and lower/slower dosing for non-induced patients.
